title: Persuasive weight of agency interpretations under Skidmore
shortTitle: Persuasive weight of agency interpretations under Skidmore
summary: Skidmore weight is the respect a court gives an agency interpretation because its reasoning and informed experience help establish the law’s meaning.
notes:
The inquiry evaluates the interpretation’s thoroughness, reasoning, consistency, relevant expertise, and other features that make it persuasive. The agency’s official responsibilities may produce knowledge useful to judges and litigants, even where the interpretation did not emerge from a formal adversarial adjudication. An agency interpretation does not become controlling merely because the agency issued it. Skidmore illustrates the distinction with the Administrator’s assessment of fire-hall employees’ sleeping, eating, and other on-call time. (Printed 930–932.)

Loper Bright retains this source of guidance while requiring independent statutory interpretation. Its majority specifically notes the potential value of interpretations adopted near enactment and maintained over time. The assigned notes ask whether that emphasis narrows or simply elaborates the broader Skidmore formulation; they do not resolve that question. Courts also must distinguish persuasive interpretation from an agency’s exercise of actual delegated policy discretion. (Printed 945, 963.)

Kisor adds a separate comparison. Chief Justice Roberts regarded many circumstances justifying deference to an agency’s own regulation as similar to circumstances making the agency persuasive, but explicitly maintained the difference between persuasion and a conditional obligation to defer. A study answer should identify the relevant source of law and the review method before applying a generic label such as “deference.” (Printed 995–996.)
